'''Paul William''' "'''Bear'''" '''Bryant''' (September 11, 1913 – January 26, 1983) was an American [[college football]] player and coach. He is considered by many to be one of the greatest college football coaches of all time, and best known as the [[head coach]] of the [[University of Alabama]] football team, the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]], from 1958 to 1982. During his 25-year tenure as Alabama's head coach, he amassed six national championships and 13 [[Southeastern Conference|conference]] championships. Upon his retirement in 1982, he held the record for the most wins (323) as a head coach in collegiate football history. The [[Paul W. Bryant Museum]], Paul W. Bryant Hall, Paul W. Bryant Drive, and [[Saban Field at Bryant–Denny Stadium ]] are all named in his honor at the University of Alabama.

He was also known for his trademark black and white [[houndstooth]] hat (even though he normally wore a plaid one), deep voice, casually leaning up against the goal post during pre-game warmups, and holding his rolled-up game plan while on the sidelines. Before arriving at Alabama, Bryant was head football coach at the [[Maryland Terrapins football|University of Maryland]], the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|University of Kentucky]], and [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M University]].

==College playing career==

Bryant Museum |language=en-US}}</ref> Since he elected to leave high school before completing his diploma, Bryant had to enroll in a [[Tuscaloosa, Alabama|Tuscaloosa]] high school to finish his education during the fall semester while he practiced with the college team. Bryant played [[End (gridiron football)|end]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Crimson Tide]] and was a participant on the school's [[1934 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|1934 national championship team]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Walsh |first=Christopher |date=May 29, 2020 |title=Daily Dose of Crimson Tide: The 1934 National Champions |access-date=March 22, 2023 |magazine=Sports Illustrated}}</ref> Bryant was the self-described "other end" during his playing years with the team, playing opposite the big star, [[Don Hutson]], who later became a star in the [[National Football League]] and a [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]r.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Christopher |date=April 11, 2015 |title=25 interesting facts about Bryant then served off North Africa, on the [[United States Army Transport]] ''[[SS California (1927)#Troop ship|SS Uruguay]]'', seeing no combat action.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bennett |first=BJ |title=Bear Bryant's Living Legacy |url=http://www.southernpigskin.com/archives/bear-bryants-living-legacy |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150829005519/http://www.southernpigskin.com/archives/bear-bryants-living-legacy/ |archive-date=August 29, 2015 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=Southern Pigskin}}</ref> On February 12, 1943, in the North Atlantic the oil tanker [[USS Salamonie|USS ''Salmonie'']] suffered a steering fault and accidentally rammed the SS ''Uruguay'' amidships. The tanker's bow made a 70-foot (21{{spaces}}m) hole in ''Uruguay''{{'}}s hull and penetrated her, killing 13 soldiers and injuring 50. The ''Uruguay''{{'}}s crew contained the damage by building a temporary bulkhead and three days later she reached Bermuda. President Franklin D. Roosevelt decorated ''Uruguay''{{'}}s Captain, Albert Spaulding, with the Merchant Marine Distinguished Service Medal for saving many lives, his ship and her cargo.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1951/06/18/archives/two-skippers-hear-sounds-of-ship-bells-one-aboard-speedy-liner-and.html|title=Two Skippers Hear Sounds of Ship Bells: One Aboard Speedy Liner and One on Farm; URUGUAY MASTER|date=June 18, 1951 |publisher=New York Times Company|accessdate=September 15, 2026}}</ref>

Bryant was later granted an honorable discharge to train recruits and coach the [[North Carolina Pre-Flight Cloudbusters football|North Carolina Navy Pre-Flight football team]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tomberlin |first=Jason |date=October 21, 2009 |title=Bear Bryant in Chapel Hill |url=http://www.lib.unc.edu/blogs/ncm/index.php/2009/10/21/bear-bryant-in-chapel-hill/ |access-date=January 15, 2012 |website=North Carolina Miscellany |publisher=UNC University Libraries}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=August 18, 1944 |title=Bear Bryant Line Coach At Carolina |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/nashville-banner-bear-bryant-line-coach/145326638/ |access-date=April 13, 2024 |work=Nashville Banner |page=16}}</ref> One of the players he coached for the Navy was the future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] quarterback [[Otto Graham]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Donahue |first=Ben |date=April 21, 2021 |title=The Life And Career Of Otto Graham (Complete Story) |url=https://www.brownsnation.com/otto-graham-profile/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322181507/https://www.brownsnation.com/otto-graham-profile/ |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=Browns Nation |language=en-US}}</ref> While in the navy, Bryant attained the rank of [[lieutenant commander]].<ref name="Barra" />{{rp|94}}

===Maryland===
[[File:Bear Bryant 1945.jpg|thumb|Bryant as Maryland head coach in 1945]]

In 1945, 32-year-old Bryant met [[Washington Redskins]] owner [[George Preston Marshall|George Marshall]] at a cocktail party hosted by the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'', and mentioned that he had turned down offers to be an assistant coach at Alabama and [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech]] because he was intent on becoming a head coach. Marshall put him in contact with [[Curley Byrd|Harry Clifton "Curley" Byrd]], the president and former football coach of the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Browning |first=Al |url=https://archive.org/details/irememberpaulbea00albr |title=I Remember Paul "Bear" Bryant |publisher=Cumberland House Publishing |year=2001 |isbn=1-58182-159-X |pages=[https://archive.org/details/irememberpaulbea00albr/page/100 100]–101 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

After meeting with Byrd the next day, Bryant received the job as head coach of the [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland Terrapins]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Shapiro |first=Leonard |date=November 27, 1981 |title=BRYANT |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1981/11/27/bryant/6bee457e-c978-4ccc-812f-52f3125b2a51/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116141523/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1981/11/27/bryant/6bee457e-c978-4ccc-812f-52f3125b2a51/ |archive-date=November 16, 2018 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US}}</ref> In his only season at Maryland, Bryant led the team to a 6–2–1 record.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1945 Maryland Terrapins Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/maryland/1945.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322183520/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/maryland/1945.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> However, Bryant and Byrd came into conflict. In the most prominent incident, while Bryant was on vacation, Byrd brought back a player that was suspended by Bryant for not following the team rules. After [[Maryland Terrapins football: 1856–1946#Bryant's brief stint|the 1945 season]], Bryant left Maryland to take over as head coach at the [[University of Kentucky]].<ref name="Time">{{Cite magazine |last=Phillips |first=B. J. |date=September 29, 1980 |title=Football's Supercoach |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,952802-4,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110704023924/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,952802-4,00.html |archive-date=July 4, 2011 |access-date=April 2, 2016 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]}}</ref>

===Kentucky===
Bryant coached at Kentucky for eight seasons. Under Bryant, Kentucky made its first bowl appearance in [[1947 Kentucky Wildcats football team|1947]] and won its first [[Southeastern Conference]] title in 1950.<ref name="bowls">{{Cite web |title=Kentucky Wildcats Bowls |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/kentucky/bowls.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121209061446/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/kentucky/bowls.html |archive-date=December 9, 2012 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> The [[1950 Kentucky Wildcats football team]] finished with a school best 11–1 record and concluded the season with a victory over [[Bud Wilkinson]]'s top-ranked [[1950 Oklahoma Sooners football team|Oklahoma Sooners]] in the [[1951 Sugar Bowl|Sugar Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1950 Southeastern Conference Year Summary |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfbconferences/sec/1950.html |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Sugar Bowl – Oklahoma vs Kentucky Box Score, January 1, 1951 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/1951-01-01-kentucky.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322184353/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/1951-01-01-kentucky.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> The final AP poll was released before bowl games in that era, so Kentucky ended the regular season ranked No. 7. Though he led Kentucky's football program to its greatest achievement, Bryant resigned after the 1953 season because he felt that [[Adolph Rupp]]'s basketball team would always be the school's primary sport. The point shaving scandal that rocked the basketball program had Kentucky focus their energy on basketball, keeping Rupp on even after it had broken the rules in 1951, causing the Wildcats to be given the [[Death penalty (NCAA)|death penalty]] for the 1952–53 season. Bryant tried to resign that year for [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas]] but the school did not let him. Rupp recommended [[C. M. Newton]], a former backup player at Kentucky in the late 1940s. Newton went on to lead the Crimson Tide to three straight SEC titles.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame: C.M. Newton |url=https://www.hoophall.com/hall-of-famers/cm-newton/#:~:text=Charles%2520Martin%2520%2522C.M.%2522%2520Newton&text=At%2520Alabama%252C%2520Newton%2520won%2520SEC,the%2520new%2520director%2520of%2520athletics. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322184805/https://www.hoophall.com/hall-of-famers/cm-newton/#:~:text=Charles%2520Martin%2520%2522C.M.%2522%2520Newton&text=At%2520Alabama%252C%2520Newton%2520won%2520SEC,the%2520new%2520director%2520of%2520athletics. |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=HoopHall.com |language=en}}</ref>

For years, Bryant was accused of racism<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Doyle |first=Andrew |date=March 1996 |title=Bear Bryant: Symbol for an Embattled South |url=http://digitalcommons.colby.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3104&context=cq |url-status=live |journal=Colby Quarterly |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=80, 83 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161203123921/http://digitalcommons.colby.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3104&context=cq |archive-date=December 3, 2016 |access-date=March 31, 2017}}</ref> for refusing to recruit black players. (He had tried to do so at Kentucky in the late 40s but was denied by then University President, Herman Donovan.)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Miller |first=Patrick |title=The Sporting World of the Modern South. |publisher=University of Illinois Press |year=2002 |page=272|isbn=0-252-07036-4 }}</ref> Bryant said that the prevailing social climate and the overwhelming presence of noted segregationist George Wallace in Alabama, first as governor and then as a presidential candidate, did not let him do this. He finally was able to convince the administration to allow him to do so, leading to the recruitment of [[Wilbur Jackson]] as Alabama's first black scholarship player who was recruited in 1969 and signed in the Spring of 1970. Junior-college transfer [[John Mitchell (American football coach)|John Mitchell]] became the first black player for Alabama in 1971 because freshmen, thus Jackson, were not eligible to play at that time. They would both be a credit to the university by their conduct and play, thus widening the door and warming the welcome for many more to follow. ==Defamation suit==
{{See also|Bobby Dodd#Georgia Tech's withdrawal from SEC}}

In 1962 Bryant filed a libel suit against ''[[The Saturday Evening Post]]'' for printing an article by [[Furman Bisher]] ("College Football Is Going Berserk") that charged him with encouraging his players to engage in brutality in a 1961 game against the [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football|Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bisher |first=Furman |date=October 20, 1962 |title=College Football is Going Berserk |url=http://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/wp-content/uploads/satevepost/satevepost-1962.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130315044829/http://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/wp-content/uploads/satevepost/satevepost-1962.pdf |archive-date=March 15, 2013 |access-date=May 27, 2013 |work=[[The Saturday Evening Post]]}}</ref> Six months later, the magazine published "The Story of a College Football Fix" that charged Bryant and [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia Bulldogs]] athletic director and ex-coach [[Wally Butts]] with conspiring to fix their 1962 game together in Alabama's favor.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Graham |first=Frank Jr. |date=March 23, 1963 |title=The Story of a College Football Fix |url=http://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/wp-content/uploads/satevepost/georgia-vs-alabama.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205110257/http://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/wp-content/uploads/satevepost/georgia-vs-alabama.pdf |archive-date=December 5, 2014 |access-date=May 27, 2013 |work=[[The Saturday Evening Post]]}}</ref> Butts also sued Curtis Publishing Co. for [[defamation|libel]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul Bryant Facts |url=http://biography.yourdictionary.com/paul-bryant |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130414221147/http://biography.yourdictionary.com/paul-bryant |archive-date=April 14, 2013 |access-date=May 27, 2013 |website=yourdictionary.com}}</ref> The case was decided in Butts' favor in the US District Court of Northern Georgia in August 1963, but Curtis Publishing appealed to the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]]. As a result of ''[[Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts]]'' 388 U.S. 130 (1967),<ref>{{ussc|Source=f|388|130|1967}}</ref> Curtis Publishing was ordered to pay $3,060,000 in damages to Butts. The case is considered a landmark case because it established conditions under which a news organization can be held liable for defamation of a "public figure". Bryant reached a separate out-of-court settlement on both of his cases for $300,000 against Curtis Publishing in January 1964.

==Legacy==
Many of Bryant's former players and assistant coaches went on to become head coaches at the collegiate level and in the [[National Football League]]. [[Danny Ford]] ([[Clemson Tigers football|Clemson]], 1981), [[Howard Schnellenberger]] ([[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami]] of Florida, 1983), and [[Gene Stallings]] (Alabama, 1992), one of the [[Junction Boys]], all won national championships as head coaches for [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] programs while [[Joey Jones (American football)|Joey Jones]], [[Mike Riley (American football)|Mike Riley]], and [[David Cutcliffe]] are active head coaches in the NCAA. [[Charles McClendon]], [[Jerry Claiborne]], [[Sylvester Croom]], [[Jim Owens]], [[Jackie Sherrill]], [[Bill Battle]], [[Bud Moore (American football)|Bud Moore]] and [[Pat Dye]] were also notable NCAA head coaches.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisband |first=Brett |date=March 30, 2015 |title=Bear Bryant's coaching tree |url=https://www.saturdaydownsouth.com/alabama-football/bear-bryants-coaching-tree/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220517012649/https://www.saturdaydownsouth.com/alabama-football/bear-bryants-coaching-tree/ |archive-date=May 17, 2022 |access-date=April 1, 2023 |website=Saturday Down South}}</ref> Croom was the SEC's first African-American head coach at [[Mississippi State Bulldogs football|Mississippi State]] from 2004 through 2008.

[[Super Bowl LV]] winning NFL head coach [[Bruce Arians]] was a running backs coach under Bryant in 1981–82.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cooper |first=Jon |date=May 23, 2018 |title=Bruce Arians tells story of time he stood up to Bear Bryant at Alabama |url=https://www.saturdaydownsouth.com/alabama-football/bruce-arians-tells-story-time-stood-bear-bryant-alabama/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221012153431/https://www.saturdaydownsouth.com/alabama-football/bruce-arians-tells-story-time-stood-bear-bryant-alabama/ |archive-date=October 12, 2022 |access-date=April 1, 2023 |website=Saturday Down South |language=en-US}}</ref> Arians also served as a successful head coach of the [[Arizona Cardinals]], leading them to just their second ever appearance in the NFC Championship Game in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weinfuss |first=Josh |date=July 19, 2016 |title=Bruce Arians didn't see Cardinals' blowout in NFC title game coming 'in a million years' |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/arizona-cardinals/post/_/id/20915/bruce-arians-didnt-see-cardinals-blowout-in-nfc-title-game-coming-in-a-million-years |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221012185438/https://www.espn.com/blog/arizona-cardinals/post/_/id/20915/bruce-arians-didnt-see-cardinals-blowout-in-nfc-title-game-coming-in-a-million-years |archive-date=October 12, 2022 |access-date=April 1, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

[[Ozzie Newsome]], who played for Bryant at Alabama from 1974 to 1977, played professional football for the Cleveland Browns for thirteen seasons (1978–1990), and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1999.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ozzie Newsome College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/ozzie-newsome-1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322191026/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/ozzie-newsome-1.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Newsome was the general manager of the Cleveland Browns-[[Baltimore Ravens]] from 1996 through 2018. Newsome was the GM of the Ravens' [[Super Bowl XXXV]] championship team in [[2000 NFL season|2000]], and their [[Super Bowl XLVII]] championship team in [[2012 NFL season|2012]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ozzie Newsome Football Executive Record |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/executives/NewsOz0.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322191049/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/executives/NewsOz0.htm |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

[[Jack Pardee]], one of the Junction Boys, played linebacker in the NFL for sixteen seasons with the [[Los Angeles Rams]] and [[Washington Redskins]], was a college head coach at the University of Houston, and an NFL head coach with Chicago, Washington, and Houston.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jack Pardee Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PardJa00.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322152203/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PardJa00.htm |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jack Pardee College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/jack-pardee-1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322152242/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/jack-pardee-1.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jack Pardee Record, Statistics, and Category Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/PardJa0.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230112185443/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/PardJa0.htm |archive-date=January 12, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Bryant was portrayed by [[Gary Busey]] in the 1984 film ''[[The Bear (1984 film)|The Bear]]'', by [[Sonny Shroyer]] in the 1994 film ''[[Forrest Gump]]'', [[Tom Berenger]] in the 2002 film ''[[The Junction Boys (film)|The Junction Boys]]'', and [[Jon Voight]] in the 2015 film ''[[Woodlawn (film)|Woodlawn]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Casagrande |first=Michael |date=June 20, 2014 |title=Controversial Bear Bryant movie has small cult following 30 years after box office bomb |url=https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/2014/06/controversial_bear_bryant_movi.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322151847/https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/2014/06/controversial_bear_bryant_movi.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=AL.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Flanagan |first=Ben |date=June 27, 2019 |title=Sonny Shroyer on playing Bear Bryant in 'Forrest Gump' |url=https://www.al.com/life/2019/06/how-enos-from-dukes-of-hazzard-became-bear-bryant-in-forrest-gump.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322151921/https://www.al.com/life/2019/06/how-enos-from-dukes-of-hazzard-became-bear-bryant-in-forrest-gump.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=AL.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Garrison |first=Greg |date=August 30, 2015 |title=Jon Voight talks about playing Bear Bryant in 'Woodlawn' |url=https://www.al.com/living/2015/08/i_have_the_greatest_respect_fo.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322151954/https://www.al.com/living/2015/08/i_have_the_greatest_respect_fo.html |archive-date=March 22, 2023 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=AL.com |language=en}}</ref> Bryant is also mentioned as one of the titular 'Three Great Alabama Icons' in the song of the same name by the [[Drive-By Truckers]] on their album ''[[Southern Rock Opera]]''.

==Head coaching record==
In his 38 seasons as a head coach, Bryant had 37 winning seasons and participated in a total of 29 postseason [[bowl game]]s, including 24 consecutively at Alabama. He won fifteen bowl games, including eight [[Sugar Bowl]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bear Bryant College Coaching Records, Awards and Leaderboards |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/coaches/bear-bryant-1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140706234430/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/coaches/bear-bryant-1.html |archive-date=July 6, 2014 |access-date=March 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Bryant still holds the records as the youngest college football head coach to win three hundred games and compile thirty winning seasons.
